As shown in the case studies, methods can range from simple upper and lower thresholds to more sophisticated statistical approaches like Kernel Density Estimation (KDE), which automatically identifies extreme values. The goal is to remove clear errors without discarding valuable data from genuine process upsets. • Data Imputation: This step addresses missing data by filling the gaps. The choice of method is critical. Simple approaches like using the average value can be effective, but more complex techniques like k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) or multivariate linear models were also explored. A key challenge here is avoiding data leakage—accidentally using future information to fill past gaps (e.g., linear interpolation), which can create a model that looks deceptively accurate in testing but fails in real-time deployment. 2.4.3 Step 2: Feature Selection – Focusing on What Matters A modern WRRF can generate thousands of data signals, but not all are relevant to the specific problem at hand. Feeding a model with irrelevant or redundant information increases its complexity, making it more prone to overfitting and harder to interpret. Feature selection is the disciplined process of identifying and retaining only the most predictive input variables (or "features"). • Techniques like analyzing Correlation Coefficients or using automated methods like minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) help to filter the noise and focus the model on the true drivers of the process. For instance, in the Application 5 (biosolids optimization), Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was exceptionally effective at reducing the high-dimensional acoustic sensor data into a manageable number of informative components.
